_comment: Feature 21 - Declarative ORM relationships. Two owner decisions:
REL-DEC-01 (OWNER-DECISIONS.md Batch 2): relationships are READ-SIDE-ONLY.
The framework wires up traversal accessors but emits NO DB-level FK /
ON DELETE clause (consistent with the no-foreign-key Firebird rule), so
referential integrity is the migration/DDL's job and deleting a parent does
NOT cascade to children at the engine level. Python's phantom `on_delete=`
parameter -- which silently did nothing -- is DROPPED: passing it now raises a
clear read-side-only error instead of implying a cascade that never happens.
PHP/Ruby/Node never had an on_delete option and emit no FK constraint, so they
were already read-side-only (code wins over the audit; verified, not 'fixed').
REL-DEC-02 (feature doc 021, the fix bundle): the traversal itself is made
correct and consistent in all four:
* REL-NODE-AUTOWIRE-DEAD (the big one): Node's DOCUMENTED declarative FK
auto-wire produced NO accessors and had NO lazy load -- post.author /
author.posts were missing and include did not populate them (the eager
grouping also mismatched an FK that round-tripped as "1.0" against an
INTEGER pk). Node now attaches belongsTo/hasMany/hasOne LAZY accessors on
both sides (reusing the imperative path + the cross-model registry) and
normalizes the eager join key, so declarative relationships FUNCTION and
match Python/PHP/Ruby. toDict serializes a relation once it has been
loaded (eager or awaited) -- a sync serializer cannot await a lazy read.
* REL-SOFTDELETE-TRAVERSAL: the soft-delete `is_deleted = 0` filter is
applied to relationship TRAVERSAL (lazy AND eager) in all four, so a
soft-deleted child is NOT returned through parent.children (Python's lazy
+ all four's eager did not filter; PHP's lazy already did via where()).
* REL-EAGER-UNBOUNDED: the eager `WHERE fk IN (...)` list is CHUNKED (one
query per <=500-parent chunk) so a huge parent set never builds an
unbounded IN list; and the lazy has_many is now PAGED/uncapped (Python's
silent 1000-cap and PHP/Ruby's 100-cap are gone -- the tail is reachable).
* REL-PHP-EAGERLOAD-STATIC: the public static ORM::eagerLoad($rows,$include)
with no $db called the INSTANCE getDb() in a static context and fatalled;
it now resolves the DB via the static resolveDb() path. (PHP's eager path
also now merges the FK registry so an FK-wired has-many resolves through
eager, matching __get's lazy merge.)
NO MOCKS. Every case drives a REAL database -- real SQLite AND the lab's real
PostgreSQL (:55432, tina4/tina4). Row presence/absence is asserted by querying
the real table; the no-N+1 invariant is proven with a REAL executed-statement
counter that instruments the real adapter's fetch (observation, not a mock);
the tail-reachable case inserts > every old cap (1001 children) and reads them
all back. Positive AND negative throughout.
Mutation-proven (per framework, restored after): neuter the lazy soft-delete
filter -> the soft-deleted-child-excluded case RED (Python/Ruby); revert PHP's
static resolveDb -> the public static eagerLoad ERRORS 'getDb() cannot be
called statically'; no-op Node's _wireRelationshipAccessors -> the
lazy-attribute-access case RED (declarative relationships dead again).
Each invariant names a REAL suite file per framework carrying the SAME case
names in each language's own idiom, which scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py
normalises and matches.
feature: 21 - Declarative ORM relationships (REL-DEC-01 read-side-only cascade + drop Python on_delete; REL-DEC-02 Node declarative auto-wire + lazy load, soft-delete traversal filter, bounded eager IN + paged lazy, PHP static eagerLoad)

invariants.rule: Eager-loading a relation via include= runs EXACTLY ONE query for that relation across all parents (batched WHERE fk IN (...)), never one query per parent (no N+1). Proven by a REAL executed-statement counter on the real adapter: loading 3 parents each with 2 children issues exactly ONE query touching the child table, and the 6 children are grouped onto the right parents. Identical in all four (Python, PHP, Ruby, Node). For PHP this also exercises the public static ORM::eagerLoad($rows, $include) with no $db (REL-PHP-EAGERLOAD-STATIC).
invariants.why: The whole point of eager loading is N+1 avoidance. Counting real adapter queries (instrumentation, not a mock) proves the batched IN is issued once per relation, not per parent. The IN list is chunked at 500 parents per query so a huge parent set stays bounded; the tested set is one chunk, hence one query.

invariants.rule: A soft-deleted child is EXCLUDED from relationship traversal -- both the lazy accessor (parent.children) and the eager include= path append the soft-delete filter (is_deleted = 0). A real soft-deleted row is COUNT=1 in the raw table (negative control) but ABSENT from the parent's children in all four.
invariants.why: REL-SOFTDELETE-TRAVERSAL: traversal must be consistent with the finders' default exclusion (feature 20). Python's lazy + all four's eager did not filter; PHP's lazy already filtered via where(). Both lazy and eager are pinned so a soft-deleted child cannot reappear through a relationship. Proven against a REAL soft-deleted row -- no mocks.

invariants.rule: A parent with more than one page of children returns ALL of them through traversal -- the tail is reachable, never silently truncated. Proven by inserting 1001 children (over every old cap: Python lazy 1000, PHP/Ruby lazy 100) and reading all 1001 back through the lazy accessor. Identical in all four.
invariants.why: REL-EAGER-UNBOUNDED: Python's lazy has_many silently capped at 1000 and PHP/Ruby at 100, losing the tail with no signal; the lazy read is now paged (uncapped) so every child is reachable, and the eager IN list is chunked so it never grows unbounded. Proven against a REAL 1001-row child set -- no mocks.

invariants.rule: Reading a declared relationship as an attribute (lazy) returns the related rows: parent.children yields the child instances and child.parent yields the parent instance, in all four. This is the REL-NODE-AUTOWIRE-DEAD proof -- Node's declarative FK auto-wire now attaches working lazy accessors on both sides (previously non-functional), matching Python/PHP/Ruby.
invariants.why: Node's documented declarative auto-wire produced NO accessors and had NO lazy load, so post.author / author.posts were missing. It now attaches belongsTo/hasMany/hasOne lazy accessors (async, cached) reusing the imperative path + the cross-model registry, so declarative relationships function four-way. Proven against a REAL database -- no mocks.

invariants.rule: Relationships are READ-SIDE-ONLY: the framework emits no DB-level ON DELETE cascade, so deleting a parent leaves its children in the database. After hard-deleting a parent that has two children, the parent row is gone (COUNT=0) but both child rows survive (COUNT=2) in all four. Referential integrity is the migration/DDL's job.
invariants.why: REL-DEC-01: no engine-level referential action is emitted (consistent with the no-FK Firebird rule). This NEGATIVE-control case proves there is no phantom cascade -- children are NOT removed by a parent delete. Proven by a raw COUNT on the real table -- no mocks.

invariants.rule: Python-only: the phantom `on_delete=` parameter on ForeignKeyField -- which silently did nothing -- is DROPPED. Declaring on_delete now RAISES a clear read-side-only ValueError ('relationships are read-side-only and emit no ON DELETE / REFERENCES clause; enforce referential integrity in your migration DDL instead') rather than misleading the developer into thinking a DB cascade is configured. PHP/Ruby/Node never accepted an on_delete option, so there is nothing to drop there.
invariants.why: REL-DEC-01 (do not ship a param that does nothing): a silent no-op parameter is a phantom API. Dropping it and failing loudly is the honest behaviour -- the error names the read-side-only contract and the remedy. This is a Python-only mechanism (the other three have no such option), so the invariant is Python-scoped.
